pos: n. (an organised body of armed men; rendering Hebrew chayil, machaneh, tsaba, Greek strateuma)
etymology: From Old French armee, from Latin armata, armed. The Hebrew words behind it are more revealing than the Latin: tsaba is a host or muster, and it is the same word that stands in the divine title LORD of hosts.
biblical_def: An army in Scripture is a mustered host, and the decisive fact about every army the Bible describes is whose it is. The title LORD of hosts makes God Himself the commander of armies, and the pattern of the histories is that Israel's numbers never decide her battles — Gideon is reduced from thirty-two thousand to three hundred precisely so that Israel cannot vaunt herself. Ezekiel's valley of dry bones ends with a resurrection described in military terms: the breath came into them “and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army” (Ezekiel 37:10) — the church raised from death is not a crowd but a formation. Joel makes the terrifying inversion explicit, describing a host that belongs to God and is deployed against His own covenant people: “the LORD shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great” (Joel 2:11). Revelation brings the theme to its end in the only battle that finally matters, where the assembled powers of the earth are gathered “to make war against him that sat on the horse, and against his army” (Revelation 19:19) — and no engagement is narrated, because none is needed. The New Testament then relocates the whole vocabulary: the Christian's warfare is real but its weapons are not carnal, and the soldier's discipline is applied to endurance under a commander who has already won.
webster_summary: A mustered host, whose outcome in Scripture is settled by whose it is rather than by its size. The dry bones rise as an exceeding great army; Joel calls the invading host the LORD's own; and at Revelation 19 the assembled kings meet an army whose battle is not even described.
webster_full: ARMY, n. [Fr. armee, from L. armata, armed.] A collection or body of men armed for war, and organized in companies, battalions, regiments and brigades, under proper officers.
2. A great number; a vast multitude; as an army of locusts or caterpillars. Joel 2.
3. In Scripture, the host of heaven; the angels and the celestial bodies, as marshalled under the LORD of hosts.
4. A body of men prepared and disciplined for battle, as distinguished from a mere multitude.
5. Figuratively, any organized force acting under one command.
scriptures: Ezekiel 37:10
So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army.
Joel 2:11
And the LORD shall utter his voice before his army: for his camp is very great: for he is strong that executeth his word: for the day of the LORD is great and very terrible; and who can abide it?
Revelation 19:19
And I saw the beast, and the kings of the earth, and their armies, gathered together to make war against him that sat on the horse, and against his army.
1 Samuel 14:6

And Jonathan said to the young man that bare his armour, Come, and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised: it may be that the LORD will work for us: for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.
corruption_summary: Military language in Scripture is handled in two opposite errors — erased as embarrassing violence, or annexed to a political programme in which the church becomes a literal army with earthly enemies.
corruption_paragraphs: The first error strips the martial vocabulary out of the faith. Hymns are edited, the armour of Ephesians 6 is treated as a regrettable metaphor, and any language of enemies, warfare, or victory is heard as aggression. But the Bible's conflict is not optional decoration; it is the plot. There is a serpent, a seed, a bruised head, and a triumph, and the New Testament's most tender epistles are also its most military — Paul writes of armour and of pulling down strong holds from a prison cell. The Christian who cannot bear the vocabulary of war has usually not made peace; he has only stopped noticing the fight.

The opposite error is the older and bloodier one: taking Israel's conquest narratives as a template for the church's dealings with flesh-and-blood opponents. Crusade, inquisition, and every subsequent attempt to advance the kingdom by the sword rest on this confusion. The New Testament forecloses it in one sentence — “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2 Corinthians 10:4) — and the Lord Jesus forecloses it before Pilate: if His kingdom were of this world, His servants would fight. The dictionary holds the classical two-kingdoms position of the Reformers: the magistrate bears the sword and the church bears the word, and a church reaching for the magistrate's weapon has abandoned its own.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsaba (host, muster — the word in LORD of hosts), chayil (force, valour, hence an army), and machaneh (camp); Greek strateuma (an armed force) and strateia (warfare, campaign).
roots_lines: Hebrew tsaba (H6635) — host, army, service; the plural stands in the divine title LORD of hosts (YHWH tseba'oth).
Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, valour, an army; the same word rendered virtuous of the woman in Proverbs 31:10.
Hebrew machaneh (H4264) — camp, encampment; the word in Joel 2:11 rendered camp.
Greek strateuma (G4753) — an armed force, army; used of the Lord's host in Revelation 19:14, 19.
Greek strateia (G4752) — a military campaign, warfare; the noun in 2 Corinthians 10:4 and 1 Timothy 1:18.
usage: “An exceeding great army” — the resurrected people of God described as a formation, not a crowd.
“There is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few” — Jonathan's principle, and the reason numbers never decide Israel's battles.
“Against him that sat on the horse, and against his army” — the last muster of the kings, and no battle narrated.

pos: n. (defensive equipment worn in battle; rendering Hebrew keli, nesheq, Greek panoplia, hopla)
etymology: From Old French armeure, Latin armatura. The KJV spelling keeps the British form. The key Greek term is panoplia — pan, all, and hopla, arms: the full kit, not a selection from it.
biblical_def: Armour is defensive equipment, and Scripture's two great passages on it teach opposite halves of one lesson. The first is negative. Saul dresses David in royal armour before Goliath, and David takes it off: “I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them” (1 Samuel 17:39). Untested armour is worse than none, and borrowed armour fits no one. The second is positive and is the Christian's standing order: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11), repeated for emphasis at verse 13 with the purpose stated three times over — to withstand, to stand, and having done all, to stand. It is worth noticing what the armour is for. It is not issued for advance, conquest, or victory; the verb Paul chooses is stand, because the victory has been won and the believer's task is to hold ground already taken. Every piece is a doctrine or a duty — truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God — so the man who neglects doctrine is not merely uninformed but unarmoured. Paul's other image supplies the ethical dimension: “let us cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light” (Romans 13:12). Armour is put on the way clothing is put on, deliberately, daily, and by the man himself.
webster_summary: Defensive equipment. David refuses Saul's untested armour; Paul commands the whole armour of God, whose stated purpose is not conquest but standing; Romans calls holiness itself the armour of light.
webster_full: ARMOR, ARMOUR, n. [L. armatura.] Defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle; formerly called harness.
2. Steel or iron covering, either wrought into a coat of mail, or in plates.
3. In Scripture, the whole apparatus of defence appointed for the Christian soldier. Eph. 6.
4. Armor-bearer, one who carries the armor of another; an office of trust in the Hebrew armies.
5. Figuratively, whatever defends or protects; as the armor of light. Rom. 13.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:11
Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.
Ephesians 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Romans 13:12
The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.
1 Samuel 17:39
And David girded his sword upon his armour, and he assayed to go; for he had not proved it. And David said unto Saul, I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him.
corruption_summary: The armour of God is treated as a devotional ritual to be recited each morning rather than as the doctrines and duties it names — and the word whole is quietly dropped, leaving Christians who have selected the pieces they like.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 6 is often taught as a visualisation: picture the helmet, picture the breastplate, name each piece aloud. The passage itself names concrete realities. The girdle is truth — actual doctrinal truth known and held. The breastplate is righteousness, which in Paul means both Christ's imputed righteousness and the practising of it. The shoes are the preparation of the gospel of peace, meaning readiness to carry it. The sword is the word of God, which cannot be wielded by a man who has not learned it. To recite the list without acquiring the things is to mime putting on equipment one does not own. The Puritans understood this and wrote at length on each piece as a doctrine to be studied; William Gurnall's treatment runs to well over a thousand pages, because the armour is the Christian faith itself and not a morning liturgy.

The other loss is the word whole. Paul says panoplia twice, the full kit, and the pieces are not optional or interchangeable. A believer may take a genuine interest in truth and neglect righteousness, or hold sound doctrine and never lift the shield of faith, and the gaps are exactly where the wiles of the devil are aimed. There is a related and opposite error in the deliverance-ministry treatment of the passage, which reads the armour as a formula conferring protection by recitation. Paul locates the danger in wiles — stratagems, deceits — and the defence in doctrine known and obeyed, which is why the sword is the word and not an incantation.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (vessel, implement, hence weapons) and nesheq (equipment, armoury); Greek panoplia (full armour, from pan + hopla) and hopla (arms, instruments).
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — article, vessel, implement; used of weapons and armour, and of the vessels of the sanctuary.
Hebrew nesheq (H5402) — equipment, weaponry, an armoury; used of Hezekiah's house of armour in Isaiah 39:2.
Greek panoplia (G3833) — full armour, the complete equipment of a heavy infantryman; used in Ephesians 6:11, 13 and Luke 11:22.
Greek hopla (G3696) — arms, instruments, weapons; the word in Romans 13:12 rendered armour and in 2 Corinthians 10:4 rendered weapons.
Greek thorax (G2382) — breastplate; the piece named for righteousness in Ephesians 6:14 and for faith and love in 1 Thessalonians 5:8.
usage: “The whole armour of God” — panoplia, the full kit; the pieces are not optional.
“Having done all, to stand” — the armour is issued for holding ground, not for taking it.
“I have not proved them” — David refuses equipment he has not tested, and kills the giant with what he has.

pos: n. (an instrument of offence in combat; rendering Hebrew keli, nesheq, Greek hoplon)
etymology: Old English waepen, of Germanic origin. Where armour is what a soldier wears, a weapon is what he uses; Scripture is emphatic that the Christian has both, and that neither is made of steel.
biblical_def: A weapon is an instrument of offence, and the New Testament's central statement about Christian weapons is a denial followed by a claim: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2 Corinthians 10:4). Both halves matter. Not carnal rules out coercion, political force, manipulation, and the whole apparatus of worldly leverage. Mighty through God rules out the pious weakness that mistakes having no sword for having no power. Paul then names the target with precision: the strong holds are arguments and pretensions — “casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). The battlefield is the mind, the fortress is a false idea, and the weapon that reduces it is the truth. Isaiah gives the corresponding promise on the defensive side, and it is a promise about outcome rather than about exemption: “No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn” (Isaiah 54:17). Weapons are formed and tongues do rise; what is denied is not the attack but its success. And Ecclesiastes adds the sober counterweight that one sinner destroys much good — the wisdom that is better than weapons of war can still be undone from within.
webster_summary: An instrument of offence. Paul denies that Christian weapons are carnal and claims they are mighty through God, aimed at arguments and pretensions; Isaiah promises not that no weapon will be formed but that none will prosper.
webster_full: WEAPON, n. wep'n. [Sax. waepen.] Any instrument of offense; any thing used or designed to be used in destroying or annoying an enemy.
2. An instrument for contest, or for annoying an enemy. The weapons of our warfare are not carnal. 2 Cor. 10.
3. In botany, a thorn, prickle or sting, with which plants are furnished.
4. Weapon-salve, a salve which was supposed to cure the wound by being applied to the weapon that made it.
5. Figuratively, any means of attack or defense, as words or arguments.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 10:4
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
2 Corinthians 10:5
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
Isaiah 54:17

No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper; and every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me, saith the LORD.
Ecclesiastes 7:12
For wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life to them that have it.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 54:17 is preached as a personal shield against all adversity, detaching it from the servants of the LORD it was given to and from the judgment-scene it describes; and 2 Corinthians 10:4 is quoted to bless whichever weapons the speaker already prefers.
corruption_paragraphs: “No weapon formed against me shall prosper” has become a talisman, recited over careers, finances, and health as a guarantee that nothing will go wrong. The verse says something better and narrower. Its setting is a courtroom — every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment — and its subject is stated at the end: the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their righteousness is of me. The promise is that no accusation will finally stand against those whose righteousness God has supplied, which is the same ground Paul stands on when he asks who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect (Romans 8:33). It does not promise that no weapon will be formed; Isaiah has just said in the previous clause that God creates the waster to destroy. It promises the verdict, not the absence of the trial — and every martyr in Hebrews 11 died with the promise intact.

2 Corinthians 10:4 suffers the reverse abuse: it is cited to endorse whatever the speaker was going to do anyway. For one camp it sanctifies retreat, as though non-carnal meant non-confrontational, when Paul in the same breath speaks of pulling down and casting down. For another it becomes a warrant for spiritual-warfare technique — binding, rebuking, and territorial mapping — that Paul never describes. His own account of the weapon is unglamorous and specific: arguments demolished, thoughts brought captive to Christ's obedience. That is preaching, teaching, apologetic, and discipline, exercised by ordinary men with an open Bible, and it is more powerful than any of the substitutes offered for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew keli (implement, hence weapon) and nesheq (armament); Greek hoplon (an implement or weapon), whose plural gives both armour in Romans 13:12 and weapons in 2 Corinthians 10:4.
roots_lines: Hebrew keli (H3627) — article, implement, weapon; the general word for equipment of any kind.
Hebrew nesheq (H5402) — weaponry, armament; the collective term for a nation's arms.
Greek hoplon (G3696) — a tool, implement, weapon; plural hopla, rendered weapons in 2 Corinthians 10:4 and instruments in Romans 6:13.
Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; the adjective Paul denies of Christian weapons.
Greek ochyroma (G3794) — a stronghold, fortress; the target in 2 Corinthians 10:4, which verse 5 identifies as arguments and pretensions.
usage: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal” — a denial and a claim: no worldly leverage, and no powerlessness either.
“Bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ” — the mind is the battlefield and the objective.
“No weapon that is formed against thee shall prosper” — the verdict is promised, not the absence of the trial.

pos: n. and adj. (one taken and held by force in war; rendering Hebrew shebi, galah, Greek aichmalotos)
etymology: From Latin captivus, from capere, to take. The Greek aichmalotos is more vivid — aichme, a spear-point, and haliskomai, to be caught: one taken at spear-point.
biblical_def: A captive is a person taken and held by a stronger power, and Scripture develops the word along three lines that converge in the gospel. Historically, captivity is the covenant curse: Israel and Judah are carried away, and the exile is the great national judgment the prophets both threaten and interpret. Spiritually, the word describes the unconverted with unsettling precision — men are “taken captive by him at his will” (2 Timothy 2:26), the devil's will and not their own, which is why the Reformed doctrine of bondage of the will is not a hard saying imposed on the text but the text's own picture. Paul's remedy in the same verse is that they may recover themselves out of the snare, granted through God giving repentance; the captive does not negotiate his release. Redemptively, Christ is the captive-taker who reverses the direction: “When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men” (Ephesians 4:8), quoting Psalm 68 — the triumphant King parades the powers that held His people and distributes spoil to the church in the form of gifted men. Isaiah 61:1 had promised liberty to the captives, and the Lord Jesus read it in Nazareth as fulfilled that day: “he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives” (Luke 4:18). And Paul turns the word once more to describe the believer's discipline, in which every thought is brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ — the only captivity that is freedom.
webster_summary: One taken and held by force. Captivity is Israel's covenant judgment; unconverted men are taken captive by the devil at his will; Christ ascends leading captivity captive and preaches deliverance to captives; and the believer's thoughts are taken captive to Christ.
webster_full: CAPTIVE, n. [L. captivus, from capio, to take.] A prisoner taken by force or stratagem in war, by an enemy.
2. One who is charmed or ensnared by beauty or excellence; one whose affections are seized.
3. A person kept in bondage.
CAPTIVITY, n. The state of being a prisoner, or of being in the power of an enemy by force or the fate of war.
5. Subjection to love; servitude; slavery; as the captivity of sin.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:26
And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.
Ephesians 4:8
Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.
Luke 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
2 Corinthians 10:5
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
corruption_summary: Luke 4:18 is read as a purely social manifesto, with the captives redefined as the politically oppressed and the deliverance as liberation from earthly structures — while 2 Timothy 2:26, which says what the captivity actually is, goes unread.
corruption_paragraphs: The Nazareth sermon is the favourite text of liberation theology, where poverty, captivity, blindness, and bruising are read as economic and political conditions and the Messiah's programme becomes the overthrow of oppressive systems. The reading has a real foothold — Scripture's concern for the poor and the oppressed is genuine and constant, and any Christianity that ignores it is defective. But the Lord Jesus interpreted His own text by what He then did, and He did not raise a militia or redistribute an estate; He forgave sins, healed bodies, cast out devils, and went to a cross. Paul supplies the definition the political reading omits: the captives are men held by the devil at his will (2 Timothy 2:26), and the deliverance is the repentance and knowledge of the truth God grants. A gospel that frees a man from a landlord and leaves him in that captivity has not read the verse it is quoting.

The opposite failure is to spiritualise Luke 4:18 so completely that it touches nothing. The jubilee background of Isaiah 61 is unmistakably material — debts released, land returned, slaves sent home — and the Lord took that vocabulary up deliberately. The right reading holds both ends: the captivity Christ breaks is first and fundamentally captivity to sin and Satan, and the freed captive is then sent back into ordinary life with obligations to the poor, the indebted, and the bruised that the jubilee law made concrete. Ephesians 4:8 shows the pattern — the ascended Christ takes captivity captive and immediately gives gifts to men, and those gifts are pastors and teachers put to work in a real congregation.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebi (captivity, a body of captives) and galah (to uncover, hence to go into exile); Greek aichmalotos (one taken at spear-point) and aichmalotizo (to take captive).
roots_lines: Hebrew shebi (H7628) — captivity, captives collectively; the noun in Psalm 68:18, quoted at Ephesians 4:8.
Hebrew galah (H1540) — to uncover, remove, carry into exile; the standard verb for the deportations of Israel and Judah.
Greek aichmalotos (G164) — a captive, from aichme (spear-point); the word in Luke 4:18.
Greek aichmalotizo (G163) — to lead captive; used both of Satan's work (Romans 7:23) and of Paul taking thoughts captive (2 Corinthians 10:5).
Greek zogreo (G2221) — to take alive, catch as game; the striking verb in 2 Timothy 2:26, the same word used of Peter catching men in Luke 5:10.
usage: “Taken captive by him at his will” — the bondage of the will stated as plainly as Scripture ever states it.
“He led captivity captive” — the ascension as a triumphal procession, with spoil distributed to the church.
“Bringing into captivity every thought” — the one captivity that is liberty.

pos: n. (a gap broken in a wall; hence a rupture, a violation; rendering Hebrew perets, pirtsah)
etymology: From Old English bryce, a breaking, related to break. The Hebrew perets is the same word that names Pharez, and the same root that names the place Perez-uzzah — Scripture builds proper names out of its breaches.
biblical_def: A breach is a gap broken in a wall, and Scripture uses the picture in three directions. It is first a judgment: when God moves against His people the language is that He makes a breach in them, as at Uzzah — “David was displeased, because the LORD had made a breach upon Uzzah” (2 Samuel 6:8) — a city wall opened is a city undefended. It is second a place where a man may stand, and this is the most striking use in the Psalter: “Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath” (Psalm 106:23). The intercessor is a man who puts his own body in the gap of a wall God Himself is breaking, and Moses did exactly that at Sinai when he offered to be blotted out instead. It is third a thing to be repaired, and Isaiah makes the repair of breaches the honourable title of a restored people: “thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” (Isaiah 58:12) — and the context is fasting done rightly, which is to say mercy, justice, and bread given to the hungry. The law also uses the word for injury requiring restitution, “Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Leviticus 24:20), the lex talionis that limits vengeance to exact proportion rather than licensing it.
webster_summary: A gap broken in a wall. God makes a breach on Uzzah in judgment; Moses stands in the breach as intercessor and turns away wrath; Isaiah names the restored people repairers of the breach; the law measures injury breach for breach.
webster_full: BREACH, n. [See Break.] The act of breaking; or state of being broken; a rupture; a break; a gap; the space between the severed parts of a solid body parted by violence; as a breach in a garment, or in a wall.
2. The violation of a law; the non-fulfillment of a contract; as a breach of covenant.
3. An opening in a coast; a bay.
4. Separation between friends by means of enmity; difference; difference of opinion.
5. Infraction; injury; invasion; as a breach upon the sacred rights of man. To stand in the breach, to expose one's self for the defense of another.
scriptures: Psalm 106:23
Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.
Isaiah 58:12

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
2 Samuel 6:8
And David was displeased, because the LORD had made a breach upon Uzzah: and he called the name of the place Perezuzzah to this day.
Leviticus 24:20
Breach for breach, eye for eye, tooth for tooth: as he hath caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him again.
corruption_summary: “Repairer of the breach” has been lifted from Isaiah 58 and made a slogan for social programmes with the fast, the confession, and the sabbath of that chapter left behind — and standing in the breach has been reduced to a phrase for general activism rather than the costly intercession Moses actually made.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 58 is a chapter about worship before it is a chapter about mercy, and the two are not separable in it. God rejects a fast conducted while men exact their labour and smite with the fist of wickedness, and He names the fast He chose: loose the bands of wickedness, deal bread to the hungry, bring the poor to your house, cover the naked. Then comes the promise of the title — repairer of the breach — and then, in the verses immediately following, the sabbath, honoured by turning away from doing one's own pleasure. Quoting the title while discarding both the repentance that precedes it and the sabbath that follows it produces exactly the fast God refused: real activity, real expenditure, and no worship. The dictionary takes the chapter whole, which is more demanding than either the activist or the ritualist reading of it.

The intercessory sense has been flattened in a different way. Psalm 106:23 describes Moses standing in a gap that God was making, pleading against a destruction God had announced, and offering himself in the place of the people — blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book (Exodus 32:32). That is a shadow of substitution, and it points to the Mediator who did not merely offer but was accepted. To use the phrase for any earnest effort in a good cause empties it. There is one Man who finally stood in the breach, and Christians stand there after Him in prayer, not in merit.
roots_summary: Hebrew perets and pirtsah (a breaking forth, a gap in a wall), from parats, to break through; the same root names Pharez (Genesis 38:29) and Perez-uzzah.
roots_lines: Hebrew perets (H6556) — a breach, gap, bursting forth; the noun in 2 Samuel 6:8 and Psalm 106:23.
Hebrew parats (H6555) — to break through, burst out; the verb behind the name Pharez in Genesis 38:29.
Hebrew pirtsah (H6556 variant) — a breach in a wall; used of the ruined walls of Jerusalem in Amos 9:11.
Hebrew gadar (H1443) — to wall up, repair a breach; the verb in Isaiah 58:12 and in Ezekiel 22:30 (make up the hedge).
Greek has no single equivalent; the Septuagint of Psalm 106:23 uses diakope, a cutting-through, for the gap Moses stood in.
usage: “Stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath” — the intercessor puts himself in the gap of a wall God is breaking.
“The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in” — the title of a people whose fast God accepted.
“Breach for breach” — the law limiting retribution to exact proportion, not licensing revenge.

pos: n. (protection, a fortification; also, a reasoned answer to a charge; rendering Hebrew misgab, tsel, Greek apologia)
etymology: From Old French defens, Latin defensus, from defendere, to ward off. The KJV spelling keeps the British form. The Greek noun on the New Testament side, apologia, is a courtroom word and gives us apologetics.
biblical_def: Defence in the Old Testament is overwhelmingly a name for God rather than a description of a wall. David does not say God provides a defence; he says “He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved” (Psalm 62:2), and again after a night of danger, “I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble” (Psalm 59:16). The Hebrew misgab means a high place out of reach — safety is elevation, not thickness of wall. The corollary appears at Kadesh, where Caleb and Joshua make the theological argument for invasion: the giants' “defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not” (Numbers 14:9). Whatever shadow protected Canaan has lifted; therefore the walls are irrelevant. Ecclesiastes brings the word down to ordinary providence with characteristic dryness: “wisdom is a defence, and money is a defence: but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom giveth life” (Ecclesiastes 7:12) — money genuinely does protect a man, and Solomon says so, but it cannot do the one thing wisdom does. In the New Testament the word turns forensic: Paul speaks of “the defence and confirmation of the gospel” (Philippians 1:7), and Peter requires every Christian to be ready to give one.
webster_summary: Protection, and in the New Testament a reasoned answer. The Psalms make God Himself the believer's defence; Caleb argues that Canaan's defence has departed; Ecclesiastes grants that money defends but cannot give life; Paul is set for the defence of the gospel.
webster_full: DEFENSE, DEFENCE, n. defens'. [L. defensus, from defendo.] Any thing that opposes attack, violence, danger or injury; fortification; guard; protection; security.
2. Vindication; justification; apology; that which repels accusation.
3. In law, the defendant's reply to the plaintiff's declaration.
4. Resistance; opposition; as, they made a vigorous defense.
5. In Scripture, God himself, as the refuge and high tower of his people. Ps. 59; Ps. 62.
scriptures: Psalm 62:2
He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved.
Psalm 59:16
But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble.
Numbers 14:9
Only rebel not ye against the LORD, neither fear ye the people of the land; for they are bread for us: their defence is departed from them, and the LORD is with us: fear them not.
Philippians 1:7
Even as it is meet for me to think this of you all, because I have you in my heart; inasmuch as both in my bonds, and in the defence and confirmation of the gospel, ye all are partakers of my grace.
corruption_summary: Defending the faith has been recast as bad manners — a failure of winsomeness — so that apologia, a duty laid on every Christian, is treated as the temperamental preference of a combative minority.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's instruction is universal and unconditional: be ready always to give an answer — apologia, a defence — to every man that asks a reason of the hope in you, with meekness and fear (1 Peter 3:15). The qualifiers govern the manner, not the fact. A generation trained to hear all disagreement as aggression has quietly converted those qualifiers into an exemption, so that the meek Christian is the one who does not answer at all. Paul, in bonds, describes his imprisonment as the defence and confirmation of the gospel and expects the Philippians to be partakers in it. Silence has its place, and there is a real folly in answering a fool according to his folly; but a church that never defends what it believes will shortly not know what it believes, since doctrines are held most firmly by those who have had to state them under pressure.

The Psalms guard the opposite ditch. He only is my rock… he is my defence forbids the apologist from mistaking his arguments for the wall. Caleb's reasoning at Kadesh is exactly right on this point: he does not say Israel is stronger, he says Canaan's protection has departed and the LORD is with us. And Ecclesiastes 7:12 keeps the accounting honest in the other direction — money really is a defence, and the man who pretends otherwise is not more spiritual, only less observant. Scripture's ordering is what matters: real second causes, genuinely protective, all of them under the one who is the defence itself.
roots_summary: Hebrew misgab (a high place, secure height, hence defence) and tsel (shadow, protection — the word in Numbers 14:9); Greek apologia (a reasoned answer given in court).
roots_lines: Hebrew misgab (H4869) — a high refuge, secure height; rendered defence in Psalm 59:9, 16-17 and high tower elsewhere.
Hebrew tsel (H6738) — shadow, shade, protection; the word in Numbers 14:9 rendered defence.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock, cliff; the companion image in Psalm 62:2, and a divine title throughout Deuteronomy 32.
Greek apologia (G627) — a verbal defence, reasoned answer; the word in Philippians 1:7, 17, 1 Peter 3:15, and Acts 22:1.
Greek bebaiosis (G951) — confirmation, establishing; the companion term in Philippians 1:7.
usage: “He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence” — the defence is a Person, not an arrangement.
“Their defence is departed from them” — Caleb's argument for invasion, and the reason walls did not matter.
“The defence and confirmation of the gospel” — a duty Paul discharged in chains, and Peter lays on every Christian.

pos: n. and v.t. (a remitting of debt or a setting free; rendering Hebrew shemittah, Greek apoluo)
etymology: From Old French relaissier, Latin relaxare, to loosen again. The Hebrew shemittah means a dropping or letting fall — the creditor opens his hand and the debt falls out of it.
biblical_def: The release is a fixed institution in Israel's law, not an occasional act of generosity: “At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release” (Deuteronomy 15:1), and the terms are spelled out in the next verse — “Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release” (Deuteronomy 15:2). Three things are worth noting. The release is periodic and predictable, so that both borrower and lender know the calendar. It is bounded by covenant kinship — brother and neighbour, with foreigners on ordinary commercial terms. And it is titled the LORD's release, which is the whole basis of it: the money was never ultimately the creditor's, any more than the land was. Moses anticipates the obvious temptation and forbids it in the same chapter, that a man's eye be evil against his poor brother as the seventh year approaches and he refuses the loan. The word then reappears in the passion narrative with terrible irony: “at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would” (Matthew 27:15). At the appointed feast, in an appointed act of release, the crowd chooses a murderer, and the innocent is bound. The pattern of substitution could not be plainer — Barabbas goes free because Jesus does not.
webster_summary: A remitting of debt or a setting free. Deuteronomy 15 makes it a fixed sabbatical institution called the LORD's release; Matthew 27 shows Pilate's customary release used to free Barabbas and bind Christ — substitution enacted in public.
webster_full: RELEASE, v.t. [Fr. relaisser; L. relaxo.] To set free from restraint of any kind, either physical or moral; to liberate from prison, confinement or servitude.
2. To free from pain, care, trouble, grief, &c.
3. To free from obligation or penalty; as, to release one from debt, from a promise or covenant.
4. To quit; to let go, as a legal claim; as, to release a debt or forfeiture.
RELEASE, n. Liberation from restraint; discharge from obligation, debt or penalty; as the year of release. Deut. 15.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 15:1
At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release.
Deuteronomy 15:2

And this is the manner of the release: Every creditor that lendeth ought unto his neighbour shall release it; he shall not exact it of his neighbour, or of his brother; because it is called the LORD'S release.
Matthew 27:15
Now at that feast the governor was wont to release unto the people a prisoner, whom they would.
Deuteronomy 31:10
And Moses commanded them, saying, At the end of every seven years, in the solemnity of the year of release, in the feast of tabernacles,
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 15 is used as a proof-text for general debt cancellation stripped of its covenantal boundaries and its accompanying command to lend generously — and in the opposite error, dismissed as expired ceremonial law with no claim on Christian mercy at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The sabbatical release is regularly enlisted for modern debt-forgiveness campaigns, and the citation usually stops before the qualifications. The law releases loans among covenant brothers, not commercial credit generally; it explicitly permits exacting from a foreigner; it presupposes an agrarian economy in which land could not be permanently alienated; and it is paired with the command not to withhold the loan in the first place as the seventh year approaches, which is a demand on the lender's heart rather than merely his ledger. Lifted out of that frame, it becomes a slogan that a creditor is a villain, which the chapter never says — the chapter says a hard-hearted creditor is a villain, and commands open-handedness before it commands cancellation.

The opposite dismissal is just as unfaithful. Israel's civil laws are not directly binding on Christians under the new covenant, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise; but the Reformed tradition has always held that their general equity continues, which is the language the confessions use. The equity here is unmistakable: God's people are not to be creditors who grind their brothers, debt is not to become a permanent status, and the poor brother has a claim on the open hand. Paul reasons the same way in 2 Corinthians 8-9 without citing the statute. And behind both stands Matthew 27:15, where a release goes to a guilty man because an innocent one was held — the pattern of every debt actually cancelled.
roots_summary: Hebrew shemittah (a dropping, letting fall, hence remission), from shamat, to let drop; Greek apoluo (to loose away, dismiss, release) and aphesis (remission, forgiveness).
roots_lines: Hebrew shemittah (H8059) — a remitting, release; the technical term for the seventh-year cancellation in Deuteronomy 15:1-2, 9.
Hebrew shamat (H8058) — to let drop, release, let rest; used of the land resting in Exodus 23:11 and of Uzzah's oxen shaking the ark.
Greek apoluo (G630) — to loose from, dismiss, set free; the verb in Matthew 27:15-26, and also the word for putting away a wife.
Greek aphesis (G859) — a sending away, remission; used of forgiveness of sins and of the liberty proclaimed in Luke 4:18.
Greek apheimi (G863) — to send away, forgive, remit; the verb in the Lord's Prayer, forgive us our debts.
usage: “It is called the LORD'S release” — the debt is remitted on God's authority because the wealth was never absolutely the creditor's.
“The solemnity of the year of release” — a fixed and public calendar, not private discretion.
“The governor was wont to release… a prisoner” — Barabbas goes free because Christ is held.

pos: v.t. and v.i. (to regain what was lost; to be restored from sickness; rendering Hebrew shub in the causative, nazal, Greek ananepho)
etymology: From Old French recovrer, Latin recuperare, to get back. The English preserves both senses Scripture uses — to regain a possession, and to return to health — and joins them to a third, the recovery of a man out of a snare.
biblical_def: To recover is to get back what was lost, and Scripture uses the word for territory, for health, and most importantly for men. David at Ziklag, having lost everything to the Amalekites, asks the Lord whether to pursue, and receives an unusually complete promise: “Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all” (1 Samuel 30:8). The passage is a study in the right order — David first encouraged himself in the LORD his God, then enquired, then pursued. Isaiah applies the word to the remnant, promising that the Lord “shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people” (Isaiah 11:11), a recovery from every direction of the compass that the New Testament sees fulfilled in the gathering of the elect from all nations. The most searching use is Paul's. Describing how a minister should deal with those who oppose themselves, he says correction is to be given in meekness, “if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will” (2 Timothy 2:25-26). The Greek ananepho means to become sober again, to come to oneself as a man does after drink — and the whole recovery is bracketed by God's giving of repentance on one side and the devil's captivity on the other. The man does return to his senses, and he could not have without the gift.
webster_summary: To regain what was lost. David recovers all at Ziklag after enquiring of the LORD; Isaiah promises the recovery of the remnant; and Paul describes captives of the devil recovering themselves — coming to sobriety — when God gives repentance.
webster_full: RECOVER, v.t. [Fr. recouvrer; L. recupero.] To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost; as, to recover stolen goods.
2. To restore from sickness; to heal; as, to recover one of a wound or disease.
3. To revive from apparent death; as, to recover a drowned person.
4. To regain by reparation or amends; as, to recover the time lost.
RECOVER, v.i. To grow well; to be restored from sickness or disorder; as, the patient recovered.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:26
And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will.
1 Samuel 30:8
And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all.
Isaiah 11:11

And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.
2 Kings 5:3
And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy.
corruption_summary: The reflexive recover themselves in 2 Timothy 2:26 is used to prove that fallen men have the native power to free themselves — a reading that severs the clause from the verse before it, where God gives the repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument is simple and superficially strong: Paul says they may recover themselves, therefore the will is free and grace is resistible in the Arminian sense. The passage will not carry it. Paul's sentence begins in verse 25 with a condition entirely outside the man — if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth — and ends in verse 26 with a bondage entirely outside his control, taken captive by the devil at his will, the devil's will and not the captive's. Between those two clauses the man does indeed come to his senses and act; that is what regeneration produces, and the Reformed doctrine has never denied that the converted man genuinely wills, chooses, and repents. What it denies is that the willing is the cause rather than the effect. The verse teaches monergism and real human agency in one breath, which is precisely the confessional position.

There is a pastoral corruption on the other side worth naming, since ministers fall into it more often. Paul frames the whole recovery as a reason for gentleness: the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. A minister who holds the doctrine of divine sovereignty and uses it to justify harshness toward the erring has taken the theology and refused the tone the same sentence commands. God's freedom to grant repentance is the reason to keep instructing patiently, not a reason to stop.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub in the hiphil (to bring back, restore) and 'asaph (to gather in, and so to heal of leprosy); Greek ananepho (to become sober again) and anablepsis (recovering of sight).
roots_lines: Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; in the causative, to bring back or recover; also the standard verb for repentance.
Hebrew 'asaph (H622) — to gather, take away; used in 2 Kings 5 of recovering Naaman of his leprosy.
Hebrew nazal, chayah (H2421) — to live, revive; used of recovery from sickness, as of Hezekiah in Isaiah 38:9.
Greek ananepho (G366) — to return to soberness, come to one's senses; the vivid hapax of 2 Timothy 2:26.
Greek anablepsis (G309) — recovering of sight; the noun in Luke 4:18, quoted from Isaiah 61.
usage: “Without fail recover all” — given to David after he encouraged himself in the LORD and enquired.
“Recover themselves out of the snare of the devil” — genuine human action, produced by repentance God gives.
“Recover the remnant of his people” — the gathering of the elect from every quarter.

pos: v.i. and n. (to utter a deep loud cry, as a lion or the sea; rendering Hebrew sha'ag, hamah, Greek oryomai)
etymology: Old English rarian, imitative in origin. Hebrew sha'ag is likewise the lion's roar, and Scripture assigns it to two figures who could not be more opposed — the LORD and the devil.
biblical_def: To roar in Scripture is the lion's cry, and the striking fact is that it belongs to God before it belongs to His enemy. Amos builds his defence of the prophetic office on it: “The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?” (Amos 3:8) — the prophet is not a volunteer, he is a man who has heard a lion in the dark and cannot keep quiet. Joel makes it the sound of the day of the LORD and, in the same breath, of refuge: “The LORD also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake: but the LORD will be the hope of his people” (Joel 3:16). The roar that shakes creation is the same voice that shelters the covenant people, which is the whole logic of the fear of the LORD — it is terror to His enemies and safety to His own. Peter then assigns the identical sound to the adversary, and the borrowing is deliberate: “your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Note the word as. The devil is not the lion; he imitates one. And the psalmist gives the word to human distress as well — the sea roars, the mountains shake, and the sons of Korah answer that God is a very present help (Psalm 46:3), so that even the roaring of chaos is set inside a psalm of confidence.
webster_summary: The lion's cry. The LORD roars from Zion and Amos cannot but prophesy; the devil merely imitates the sound, walking about as a roaring lion; and when the waters roar, the psalmist says God is a very present help.
webster_full: ROAR, v.i. [Sax. rarian.] To cry with a full, loud, continued sound; to bellow, as a beast; as, a roaring lion.
2. To cry aloud, as in distress; to bawl.
3. To make a loud noise, as the wind, the sea, thunder, or cannon.
ROAR, n. A full, loud sound of some continuance; the cry of a beast.
5. The loud continued sound of the waves or the wind; clamor; outcry.
scriptures: Amos 3:8
The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?
Joel 3:16

The LORD also shall roar out of Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the heavens and the earth shall shake: but the LORD will be the hope of his people, and the strength of the children of Israel.
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
Psalm 46:3
Though the waters thereof roar and be troubled, though the mountains shake with the swelling thereof. Selah.
corruption_summary: The devil's roar is treated as though it were his power rather than his advertisement — producing on one side a fearful Christianity that sees him everywhere, and on the other a dismissal of his existence altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter's comparison is exact and is usually flattened. He does not call the devil a lion; he says he walks about as a roaring lion, which is a statement about menace rather than about might. The true Lion of the tribe of Judah has already prevailed (Revelation 5:5), and the adversary's roar is the sound of a defeated power trying to induce despair. Peter's prescribed response confirms it: be sober, be vigilant, resist stedfast in the faith — and know that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren throughout the world. Sobriety and vigilance, not panic and not technique. Where a ministry teaches Christians to attribute every difficulty to demonic assault and to spend their prayers on rebuking, it has made the roar into a power it is not, and has left the flock more frightened than Peter left them.

The opposite corruption is more respectable and equally unbiblical: the demythologising of the devil into a symbol for social evil or psychological conflict. Scripture treats him as a personal adversary with a will, a strategy, and captives (2 Timothy 2:26), and the Lord Jesus addressed him directly. The Reformed tradition has never been credulous about the devil — Calvin warns repeatedly against a curiosity that magnifies him — but it has always been realistic. The right posture is Amos's: there is a roar in the world that must be feared, and it comes from Zion, not from the pit.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'ag (to roar, as a lion) and hamah (to murmur, roar, be tumultuous, as the sea); Greek oryomai (to howl or roar), a hapax in 1 Peter 5:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'ag (H7580) — to roar as a lion; used of the LORD in Amos 3:8, Joel 3:16, and Hosea 11:10.
Hebrew she'agah (H7581) — a roaring; used of David's cries in Psalm 22:1 and Psalm 32:3.
Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, growl, be in tumult; used of the roaring sea in Psalm 46:3.
Greek oryomai (G5612) — to howl, roar; the participle in 1 Peter 5:8, occurring nowhere else in the New Testament.
Greek leon (G3023) — lion; applied both to the devil (1 Peter 5:8) and to Christ, the Lion of the tribe of Juda (Revelation 5:5).
usage: “The lion hath roared, who will not fear?” — Amos's account of why a man prophesies: he has heard something.
“As a roaring lion” — the as is the whole point; the devil imitates a Lion who has already prevailed.
“Though the waters thereof roar” — the roaring of chaos set inside a psalm of confidence.

pos: v.t. (to take down the throat; to engulf, consume utterly; rendering Hebrew bala, Greek katapino)
etymology: Old English swelgan, to swallow. The Hebrew bala is the word for the earth opening on Korah and for the sea covering Pharaoh — and Isaiah takes that terrible verb and turns it against death itself.
biblical_def: To swallow up in Scripture is to engulf and abolish, and the verb has a career that runs from judgment to gospel. It first belongs to the earth: at Korah's rebellion Moses stakes his commission on a sign, that the ground should “open her mouth, and swallow them up” (Numbers 16:30) — the same verb Exodus uses of the sea swallowing Pharaoh's host. Then Isaiah performs the great reversal. The devourer becomes the devoured: “He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces” (Isaiah 25:8). Death, which has swallowed every generation, is itself taken down. Paul quotes it at the climax of the resurrection chapter, where the tense has moved from promise to accomplished fact: “then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), and he writes elsewhere of the believer's longing “that mortality might be swallowed up of life” (2 Corinthians 5:4) — not that the body should be shed but that it should be so overwhelmed by life that death has nothing left to take. The Lord Jesus uses the word for a different and unforgettable purpose, describing scrupulous men who filter their drink and miss the point entirely: “Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” (Matthew 23:24) — meticulous about the smallest unclean thing, and ingesting the largest.
webster_summary: To engulf utterly. The earth swallows Korah and the sea swallows Pharaoh; then Isaiah reverses the verb — God swallows up death in victory, quoted by Paul at the resurrection; and Christ mocks the guides who strain a gnat and swallow a camel.
webster_full: SWALLOW, v.t. [Sax. swelgan.] To take into the stomach; to receive through the gullet or esophagus into the stomach; as, to swallow food or drink.
2. To absorb; to draw and sink into an abyss or gulf; to ingulf; usually followed by up. The earth opened and swallowed them up. Num. 16.
3. To seize and waste; to exhaust; to consume.
4. To receive or embrace, as opinions or belief, without examination or scruple; to receive implicitly.
5. To occupy; to employ. Swallowed up in victory. 1 Cor. 15.
scriptures: Isaiah 25:8
He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the LORD hath spoken it.
1 Corinthians 15:54
So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
2 Corinthians 5:4
For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.
Matthew 23:24
Ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel.
corruption_summary: “Death is swallowed up in victory” is read at funerals as a statement that death is natural and harmless — the opposite of Paul's meaning, in which death is an enemy destroyed by an act of God, not a friend accepted.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern funeral rhetoric works hard to domesticate death: it is a part of life, a natural transition, a return to the cycle of things. Paul's language forbids it. Death in 1 Corinthians 15 is the last enemy that shall be destroyed (v. 26), it has a sting, and the sting is sin, and the strength of sin is the law. The verse quoted at gravesides is a battle report, not a reconciliation with mortality. That is why the Christian is permitted to grieve — Jesus wept at a tomb He was about to open — while grieving differently from those who have no hope. A comfort that requires pretending death is not an enemy will fail exactly when it is needed. The comfort Paul offers requires no pretending at all: the enemy is real, and it has been swallowed.

The other misuse is subtler and belongs to the over-realised eschatology that treats the victory as already complete in the believer's experience. Paul is careful with his tenses: the saying is brought to pass when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, at the last trump. Until then Christians die, and 2 Corinthians 5:4 has them groaning and burdened. A teaching that promises the swallowing-up of mortality now — freedom from sickness and infirmity as a present right — contradicts the apostle who left Trophimus at Miletum sick. And Matthew 23:24 supplies the standing warning against the scrupulosity that so often accompanies these systems: it is entirely possible to be exacting about small things while swallowing something enormous.
roots_summary: Hebrew bala (to swallow down, engulf); Greek katapino (to drink down, swallow up) and diulizo (to strain through a filter, the verb behind strain at a gnat).
roots_lines: Hebrew bala (H1104) — to swallow, engulf; used of the earth at Korah (Numbers 16:30), the sea at the Red Sea (Exodus 15:12), and death in Isaiah 25:8.
Hebrew netsach (H5331) — victory, perpetuity; the noun in Isaiah 25:8 rendered victory.
Greek katapino (G2666) — to drink down, swallow up; used in 1 Corinthians 15:54, 2 Corinthians 5:4, and of the whale in Jonah's account.
Greek diulizo (G1368) — to strain through, filter out; the verb in Matthew 23:24, rendered strain at in the KJV.
Greek nikos (G3534) — victory; the word Paul uses three times in 1 Corinthians 15:54-57.
usage: “He will swallow up death in victory” — the devourer devoured; the verb of Korah and Pharaoh turned against death.
“That mortality might be swallowed up of life” — not the shedding of the body but its overwhelming by life.
“Strain at a gnat, and swallow a camel” — scrupulous in the trivial, indiscriminate in the enormous.
